plays.title: Build movement into an ordinary week
plays.text: Start with a walk, a wheelchair-accessible route, or another activity you can repeat. Work toward 150 minutes of moderate activity each week plus muscle-strengthening activity on two days. Short sessions count; some movement is better than none. Choose a safe starting level and adapt around disability, pain, or medical restrictions. Put the next session on your calendar before buying equipment or joining a gym.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 10 minutes to choose a routine; walking or home exercises can cost $0. Build time gradually.
plays.payoff: Supports physical and mental health and helps preserve strength for everyday tasks.
plays.basis: Guidance. [CDC: Adult activity recommendations](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/guidelines/adults.html).

plays.title: Protect a realistic sleep window
plays.text: Set a wake-up time you can usually keep, then allow enough time in bed for your age and needs. Most adults need at least seven hours of sleep; older adults' recommended ranges vary. Reduce late caffeine and make the room dark, quiet, and comfortable. If you regularly struggle to sleep or remain sleepy despite enough time in bed, bring a short sleep diary to a clinician.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 15 minutes to adjust your evening routine; no device or subscription required.
plays.payoff: Adequate, refreshing sleep supports attention, mood, and health; a diary can make persistent problems easier to discuss.
plays.basis: Guidance. [CDC: About sleep](https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/).

plays.title: Make a supported plan to quit smoking
plays.text: Choose a quit date or a first planning appointment, identify your usual smoking triggers, and arrange support before cravings arrive. Review nicotine replacement and prescription options with a pharmacist or clinician, especially if pregnant or managing other conditions. A previous unsuccessful attempt provides information about what to change next. Use Smokefree's planning and support tools, and ask your health plan which counseling and medications it covers.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 20–30 minutes to start; counseling, medication prices, and insurance coverage vary.
plays.payoff: A structured quit attempt gives you tools for withdrawal and reduces continued exposure to tobacco smoke.
plays.basis: Guidance; Practice. [Smokefree: Ways to quit smoking](https://smokefree.gov/tools-tips/quit-methods).

plays.title: Choose preventive care for your age and risks
plays.text: Bring your family history, prior screening results, and vaccination record to a primary care visit. Ask which screenings and vaccines are due, which can wait, and how results would change care. Recommendations depend on age, prior results, pregnancy, exposures, and health conditions. Use current guidance rather than a fixed annual testing package. Confirm coverage before scheduling elective services; a recommended service is not automatically free in every billing situation.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 30 minutes to collect records; visit and testing costs depend on your plan and providers.
plays.payoff: Helps you complete relevant prevention while avoiding unnecessary repeat tests and unclear follow-up.

plays.title: Keep dental care simple and consistent
plays.text: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and clean between teeth regularly, aiming for daily. Use an interdental tool you can handle comfortably if floss is difficult. Arrange dental checkups at an interval matched to your risk, and mention dry mouth, diabetes, or other factors that may change care. Before an expensive proposed treatment, ask what problem it addresses, how urgent it is, and whether a less costly option is appropriate.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: several minutes daily and basic supplies; professional care prices and dental benefits vary.
plays.payoff: Supports healthy teeth and gums and helps you make informed choices about larger dental expenses.
plays.basis: Guidance; Practice. [NIDCR: Oral hygiene](https://www.nidcr.nih.gov/health-info/oral-hygiene).

plays.title: Save crisis contacts before you need them
plays.text: Save 988 in your phone and share it with someone you trust. You can call or text for emotional distress, suicidal thoughts, or substance-related concerns; a crisis counselor can also help when you are worried about someone else. Call 911 for immediate physical danger, an overdose, or another medical emergency. During a difficult period, decide who you can contact and where you can go for support.
plays.cost: The 988 service is free and available around the clock. Planning estimate: five minutes to save contacts.
plays.payoff: Makes it easier to reach a real person during a crisis without searching for a local provider first.
plays.basis: Guidance; Practice. [988 Lifeline: Get support](https://988lifeline.org/). [911.gov: Calling 911](https://www.911.gov/calling-911/).

plays.text: If cost or a long wait is blocking care, contact a nearby HRSA-supported health center and ask about mental health or substance use services, sliding fees, and referral options. plays.title: Count alcohol honestly and plan a safer change
plays.text: Track what you actually drink for a week, including serving size and alcohol strength; a large beer or cocktail may contain multiple standard drinks. Use the NIAAA tools to decide whether to reduce or stop. Avoid drinking when pregnant or when medications or health conditions make it unsafe. If you drink heavily and may be physically dependent, get medical advice before stopping abruptly because withdrawal can be dangerous.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: one minute per drinking occasion to log consumption; discussing treatment may involve a visit charge.
plays.payoff: Makes patterns visible and helps you choose a safer, more realistic change with appropriate support.
plays.basis: Guidance; Practice. [NIAAA: Rethinking Drinking](https://rethinkingdrinking.niaaa.nih.gov/). [NIAAA: Cut down or quit?](https://rethinkingdrinking.niaaa.nih.gov/thinking-about-change/cut-down-or-quit).

plays.title: Keep naloxone available when opioid exposure is possible
plays.text: Ask a pharmacist or local health department about naloxone if you or someone close to you uses opioids or could encounter an overdose. Learn the product instructions and show others where it is kept. If someone cannot be awakened and is breathing slowly or abnormally, give naloxone if available and call 911. Follow dispatcher instructions for breathing support or CPR, and stay until help arrives even if the person improves.
plays.cost: Prices and free community programs vary. Planning estimate: 15 minutes to learn the instructions and check storage.
plays.payoff: Can reverse an opioid overdose while emergency help is on the way; it does not replace that help.
plays.basis: Guidance. [CDC: Five things to know about naloxone](https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/reversing-overdose/about-naloxone.html).

plays.title: Build a small routine and notice when it is not enough
plays.text: Choose one manageable daily action: a short walk, a regular meal, a relaxing activity, or a check-in with someone supportive. Schedule it rather than waiting to feel motivated. Notice whether mood, concentration, sleep, or functioning is worsening. Seek professional help for persistent or distressing symptoms, especially around two weeks or longer; you do not need to wait two weeks if symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening, or involve safety concerns.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 5–20 minutes daily; many options cost nothing and can be adapted to your circumstances.
plays.payoff: Supports well-being and helps you recognize when additional care is needed.

plays.title: Call 911 promptly and give a usable location
plays.text: Call 911 when someone needs immediate emergency assistance. State the exact location, callback number, and what happened, then answer the dispatcher's questions and follow instructions. Put the phone on speaker if you need your hands free. At home, make sure household members know the address, unit number, and access details. Keep an emergency contact and medication list accessible without delaying a call to gather documents.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 10 minutes to prepare household information. Ambulance and emergency treatment charges depend on circumstances and coverage.
plays.payoff: Helps responders find you and lets the dispatcher guide immediate care while help is being sent.

plays.title: Learn CPR and find the nearest AED
plays.text: Take a CPR/AED course and notice where AEDs are located at work and places you visit. If a teen or adult suddenly collapses, is unresponsive, and is not breathing normally, call 911, send someone for an AED, and begin chest compressions as directed. For this situation, hands-only CPR is a useful bystander response. Turn on the AED and follow its prompts; training should also cover when rescue breaths matter.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: a few hours for training; fees vary, and some community sessions are free.
plays.payoff: Prepares you to provide immediate help during cardiac arrest before emergency responders arrive.

plays.title: Treat stroke and heart-attack symptoms as time-critical
plays.text: Call 911 for sudden facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty, or other sudden stroke signs, even if they improve. Note when symptoms began or when the person was last well. Chest pressure, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw, or back can signal a heart attack; symptoms are not always dramatic. Do not drive yourself or wait for certainty. Let emergency professionals direct the next steps.
plays.cost: Preparation estimate: 10 minutes to review warning signs with family; emergency care costs vary.
plays.payoff: Reduces delay in reaching treatments for conditions where prompt medical evaluation matters.

plays.title: Save Poison Help and call before symptoms appear
plays.text: Save Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222. If a medicine, household chemical, or other substance may have poisoned someone, call promptly rather than waiting for symptoms. Have the product container, approximate exposure time, and the person's age available if possible. For someone who is not breathing or is in immediate danger, call 911 first. Avoid home treatments such as activated charcoal unless a poison professional specifically directs you.
plays.cost: The Poison Help call is toll-free. Planning estimate: two minutes to save the number and share it with caregivers.
plays.payoff: Provides exposure-specific advice and helps determine what level of care is needed.
plays.basis: Guidance. [HRSA Poison Help: What you can do](https://poisonhelp.hrsa.gov/what-you-can-do).

plays.title: Practice how to control severe bleeding
plays.text: Take an ACS Stop the Bleed course so you can recognize dangerous bleeding and practice direct pressure, wound packing, and a tourniquet. In an emergency, check that the scene is safe, call 911, and apply firm, continuous pressure to the bleeding wound with gauze or a clean cloth. Use protective gloves if available. Follow dispatcher instructions and your training; specialized techniques need correct placement and continued pressure.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: about an hour for introductory training, plus practice; class and supply costs vary by location.
plays.payoff: Gives you practical actions to limit life-threatening blood loss while emergency help is coming.

plays.title: Compare a full year of costs before choosing a plan
plays.text: Compare annual premiums, deductibles, copays, coinsurance, and the out-of-pocket maximum using each plan's Summary of Benefits and Coverage. Estimate both an ordinary year and a year with substantial covered care. Check your doctors, hospitals, and prescriptions before choosing. Premiums, noncovered services, and some out-of-network charges generally sit outside the out-of-pocket limit. A low premium is useful only if the plan also fits your care needs and available cash.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 60–90 minutes during enrollment; gather last year's usage and your current medication list.
plays.payoff: Helps you choose coverage you can use and budget for, without assuming the cheapest premium means the cheapest care.

plays.text: After losing coverage, moving, marrying, or having a child, check promptly whether you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. Eligibility, documentation, and deadlines depend on the event and coverage source. Medicaid and CHIP accept applications year-round, with state-specific eligibility rules. Start at HealthCare.gov or your state's official marketplace and coordinate effective dates before canceling existing coverage. Revisit the choices at renewal because plans, prices, and household circumstances change.

plays.title: Appeal a denial using the reason and deadline
plays.text: Read the denial notice and identify the exact reason: missing information, a coverage exclusion, medical necessity, or another issue. Ask the clinician's office for relevant records and submit an internal appeal through the plan's stated process. Keep a copy and proof of submission. Ask about expedited review if delay could seriously harm your health. If the denial stands, check eligibility for independent external review; the process differs across private plans, Medicare, and Medicaid.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: one to three hours for an initial organized appeal; medical records and additional reviews may take longer.
plays.payoff: Gives a disputed decision a documented review without assuming that the first denial is final.

plays.title: Keep one medication list and check changes
plays.text: List each prescription, over-the-counter medicine, vitamin, and supplement, including dose, schedule, purpose, and allergies. Bring it to appointments and ask a pharmacist to review additions for interactions or duplicate ingredients. Update it after hospital discharge or a prescription change. Ask what to do about missed doses or side effects rather than improvising. plays.title: Check recalls and schedule the remedy

Follow the manufacturer's instructions for any open recall, including urgent restrictions on driving or parking. Contact an authorized dealer to confirm the remedy, availability, and coverage. A clear search result is not proof the vehicle has no problems: the tool can omit very recent recalls, older campaigns, and certain manufacturers. plays.cost: The lookup and alerts are free; estimate 10 minutes. Repair scheduling can take longer; ask the dealer about the specific remedy and any associated logistics.

plays.title: Ask about protected leave before using up your options

Federal FMLA provides eligible employees of covered employers with unpaid, job-protected leave for qualifying reasons, generally up to 12 workweeks. Eligibility includes service, hours, and worksite tests; special rules exist. Ask separately about paid sick time, disability benefits, and state family-leave programs, because job protection and wage replacement are different questions.
plays.cost: Free to inquire; estimate an hour for initial paperwork, plus possible medical certification costs.
plays.payoff: Helps preserve employment and coverage while you plan how to replace missed income.

plays.title: Put Medicare enrollment on the calendar before age 65
plays.text: Most people first become eligible around 65; the usual initial window spans seven months around that birthday month. Confirm your exact dates with Medicare. plays.text: Use shade and protective clothing when outdoors and apply a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher to exposed skin. Reapply according to the label, including after swimming or sweating. Avoid tanning beds. Pick a sunscreen you can comfortably use rather than an expensive routine you abandon. Ask a clinician about a changing or concerning skin spot; cosmetic creams cannot determine whether a lesion is harmless.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: a few minutes to prepare for outdoor time; prices vary, and clothing or shade can reduce exposed area.
plays.payoff: Reduces ultraviolet exposure and helps prevent sun damage without needing a complicated product routine.
plays.basis: Guidance; Practice. [American Academy of Dermatology: Prevent skin cancer](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/how-to-prevent).

plays.chapterTitle: Safer Weight Management and Appearance Choices
plays.title: Treat cosmetic injections as a medical procedure
plays.text: Before fillers or similar procedures, verify the professional's license, relevant training, exact product, approved use, complication plan, and follow-up arrangements. Ask what improvement is realistic and whether removal would be possible. Do not buy injectable fillers for self-injection or use a needle-free filler device at home. Severe pain, vision changes, or unusual skin discoloration during or after a filler procedure need immediate medical attention. Price alone cannot establish safety.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: one consultation before committing; include repeat treatments and potential complication care in the budget.
plays.payoff: Helps you make an informed appearance decision and recognize complications that should not wait.

plays.chapterTitle: Safer Weight Management and Appearance Choices
plays.title: Understand the lifetime commitment of cosmetic dentistry
plays.text: Before veneers, ask a licensed dentist which teeth need treatment, how much enamel would be removed, and what alternatives could achieve your goal. Veneers can require irreversible tooth preparation and eventual repair or replacement. Request an itemized plan and ask how gum disease, tooth grinding, and existing decay affect suitability. Take time for an independent opinion before extensive elective work. Keep routine prevention in place regardless of whether you choose a cosmetic procedure.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: one or two consultations; ask about future maintenance costs and confirm coverage, which may exclude cosmetic work.
plays.payoff: Makes the long-term dental consequences visible before committing healthy teeth and substantial money.

plays.title: Match STI prevention and testing to your actual exposures
plays.text: Use condoms or other appropriate barriers correctly and consistently, recognizing that protection is incomplete for infections spread through uncovered skin. Discuss partners, sexual practices, symptoms, and relevant exposures honestly with a clinician so testing covers the right infections and body sites. A urine test does not automatically cover throat or rectal infections. Ask when to test and whether repeat testing is needed after the particular exposure.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 15 minutes to locate a clinic and discuss costs; free or reduced-cost testing depends on local programs.
plays.payoff: Makes prevention and testing more relevant than ordering an unspecified 'full panel' and assuming everything is covered.
plays.basis: Guidance. [CDC: Condom use](https://www.cdc.gov/condom-use/index.html). [CDC: Getting tested for STIs](https://www.cdc.gov/sti/testing/).

plays.title: Act immediately after a possible HIV exposure
plays.text: After a possible HIV exposure, contact an emergency department, urgent care, or a clinician immediately to ask about post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP. It must start within 72 hours, and earlier is better; do not wait for symptoms or a partner's test result before seeking evaluation. If exposures may recur, ask about pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. PrEP needs appropriate testing and follow-up and does not prevent other sexually transmitted infections.
plays.cost: Seek evaluation promptly; medicine, visit charges, and assistance programs vary. Planning estimate: save a local care option in advance.
plays.payoff: Helps you use time-sensitive HIV prevention and consider an ongoing prevention plan when appropriate.

plays.title: Choose contraception around your preferences and health
plays.text: Compare methods by effectiveness, side effects, medical suitability, cost, privacy, reversibility, and how much daily attention you want to give them. Ask what starting, stopping, or removing the method involves. Your preference matters, including the choice not to use a method. Most contraceptives do not protect against STIs. After unprotected sex or a method failure, ask promptly about emergency contraception because options and effectiveness depend on timing and circumstances.

plays.payoff: Helps you select a method you can use comfortably and know what to do if it fails.

plays.title: Make consent explicit and stop when it is absent
plays.text: Check that everyone freely agrees to the sexual activity and can make that choice. A relationship, previous sex, clothing, silence, or pressure does not establish consent. Respect a change of mind and stop if someone cannot or does not agree. After an assault, prioritize immediate safety and seek medical care promptly for injuries, pregnancy prevention, and infection-related care. A sexual-assault support service can explain local options without making the decision for you.
plays.cost: A consent conversation costs nothing. After assault, medical, advocacy, and reporting options differ locally; ask about confidential support.
plays.payoff: Supports bodily autonomy and helps people access timely care and support after harm.

plays.title: Get timely, noncoercive help with pregnancy options
plays.text: After a positive pregnancy test, contact a qualified health professional to discuss your health, pregnancy timing, and options: parenting, adoption after continuing the pregnancy, or abortion. Ask which services the provider actually offers or can refer for, what costs apply, and how soon a decision affects available care. Abortion access and legal requirements vary by state and can change; verify current rules where care will occur rather than relying on an old map.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 30 minutes to identify qualified care and request an appointment; clinical costs and travel needs vary.
plays.payoff: Provides information while choices are time-sensitive and keeps your preferences central to the decision.

plays.title: Allow grief to vary and choose support that fits
plays.text: After a death or major loss, expect that feelings and energy may change from day to day. You do not need to follow a fixed sequence of stages or match someone else's timetable. Choose a trusted person, a grief group, a faith community if relevant, or a counselor who can listen without pushing you to 'move on.' Tell supporters whether you want company, conversation, or help with a practical task.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: one short message to someone you trust; group and counseling costs vary, with some community support free.
plays.payoff: Creates support that fits your needs and reduces pressure to perform recovery for other people.
plays.basis: Guidance; Practice. [NIH Clinical Center: Loss, grief, and bereavement](https://clinical.nih.gov/introduction-loss-grief-and-bereavement).

plays.title: Make a minimum plan for the next few days
plays.text: When life is disrupted, write a short plan covering meals, medicines, sleep, essential appointments, and one person to contact. Ask for concrete help such as a grocery pickup or a ride, and pause optional commitments. Reduce repeated exposure to upsetting news if it is making functioning harder. This is a temporary way to keep basic needs covered; persistent inability to eat, sleep, or care for yourself needs professional attention.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 10–15 minutes to make the plan, then a brief daily check; practical help may be shared.
plays.payoff: Keeps essential routines visible while leaving room for recovery and assistance.

plays.title: Address working conditions when burnout persists
plays.text: Identify what is making work unsustainable: workload, unpredictable hours, lack of control, conflict, or missing resources. Document concrete examples and ask for a specific change, such as a priority review, adjusted schedule, or clearer responsibilities. Use a trusted manager, HR, union, or employee assistance program as appropriate. Review available leave and accommodation options in [Chapter 13](13-work-pay-and-benefits.md). Personal relaxation can help, but it cannot by itself fix an unsafe or chronically unmanageable workload.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 30 minutes to document the problem and prepare a request; workplace responses and protections vary.
plays.payoff: Focuses the discussion on changes to the job rather than adding another self-care task to an overloaded day.

plays.title: Separate urgent obligations from irreversible decisions
plays.text: After a major loss, make two lists: tasks with real near-term deadlines and choices that can wait. Get help checking bills, documents, and appointments, but give yourself time before an optional move, major purchase, or job change. If a decision cannot wait, ask a trusted person to review the options with you and write down the reason for your choice. Postponement should not mean ignoring legal, housing, or financial deadlines.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 20 minutes for the first list and a weekly review; professional advice may have a fee.
plays.payoff: Reduces decision overload and preserves flexibility while you handle genuinely urgent responsibilities.

plays.chapterTitle: Evaluate Health Claims and Avoid Low-Value Care
plays.title: Check the evidence before buying the health claim
plays.text: Before purchasing a test, supplement, app, or treatment, identify who wrote the claim, who benefits financially, when it was updated, and what evidence supports it. Look for research in people and outcomes that matter, not only testimonials or a plausible biological story. Check an independent clinical or public-health source. A confident video or AI answer can help you form questions, but it should not settle a consequential medical decision.
plays.cost: Planning estimate: 10–20 minutes for a basic source check; public health information is usually free to read.
plays.payoff: Helps you avoid paying for claims whose evidence is weaker than their advertising.

plays.text: Ask what specific problem a supplement is meant to address, whether there is evidence for that use, and how you will know it is helping. plays.title: Question whole-body CT screening when you have no symptoms

plays.title: Check whether liability limits match your exposure
plays.text: Review the liability limits on your auto and homeowners or renters policies, then ask what an umbrella policy would add. Request its required underlying coverage, exclusions, and treatment of defense costs in writing. Consider your assets, household drivers, property use, and ability to absorb a claim. An umbrella generally addresses liability to others; it is not a substitute for coverage that repairs your own car or home.
plays.cost: Estimate: 30–60 minutes for an initial coverage review and quotes; the total may include higher limits on underlying policies.
plays.payoff: You can assess a potentially large uninsured liability instead of comparing umbrella premiums in isolation.
plays.basis: Guidance / Practice. Coverage depends on the underlying and umbrella contracts. [NAIC explanation of umbrella insurance](https://content.naic.org/article/whats-umbrella-policy).

plays.chapterTitle: Insure the losses you cannot comfortably absorb
plays.title: Identify flood and earthquake gaps before a disaster
plays.text: Read the exclusions in your property policy and ask the insurer to explain flood, earthquake, sewer backup, and wind coverage separately. Standard homeowners and renters policies commonly exclude flood and earthquake losses. Get quotes and effective dates for relevant separate policies or endorsements before deciding what to retain yourself. Include belongings and temporary housing in the discussion; a lender's insurance requirement is not a complete assessment of your exposure.
plays.cost: Estimate: one hour to review exclusions and request options; premiums, deductibles, availability, and waiting periods vary by location and policy.
plays.payoff: You can see which plausible losses would remain your responsibility and plan around those gaps.
plays.basis: Guidance / Practice. Specific exclusions and exceptions are contractual. [NAIC guide to common insurance exclusions](https://content.naic.org/article/consumer-insight-my-insurance-doesnt-cover-what).

plays.chapterTitle: Insure the losses you cannot comfortably absorb
plays.title: Review coverage when your household changes
plays.text: Set an annual reminder and revisit policies after a move, marriage, divorce, birth, major renovation, or change in household drivers. Update beneficiaries and a photo inventory of possessions. Ask whether property limits reflect rebuilding and replacement costs, and distinguish replacement-cost coverage from depreciated actual cash value. Compare the same coverage when shopping. Keep current policies until replacement coverage is confirmed effective, with any remaining gaps understood.
plays.cost: Estimate: one to two hours annually; an inventory can be built gradually with a phone and stored securely away from the property.
plays.payoff: Coverage can keep pace with your household, while comparable quotes make price differences easier to interpret.
plays.basis: Guidance / Practice. [NAIC policy review checklist](https://content.naic.org/article/consumer-insight-it-time-review-your-policies), [NAIC homeowners insurance guide](https://content.naic.org/consumer/homeowners-insurance.htm).

plays.chapterTitle: Make major commitments with a full-cost plan
plays.title: Compare renting and buying over your likely stay
plays.text: Estimate how long you could realistically stay in a home, including a job change or family move. Compare rent with ownership costs, transaction costs at both ends, repairs, and the use of your down payment elsewhere. Run scenarios with flat or falling sale prices and an earlier departure. A rent-versus-buy calculator is a way to inspect assumptions, not a prediction that ownership will make money.
plays.cost: Estimate: two to three hours to gather local quotes and model several scenarios; inspecting a real property and obtaining professional advice can add costs.
plays.payoff: You can assess whether the expected stay and cash reserves support the commitment, including an inconvenient move.
plays.basis: Guidance / Practice. [CFPB guide to deciding when to buy](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/prepare/consider-whether-its-the-right-time-for-you-to-buy/).

plays.chapterTitle: Make major commitments with a full-cost plan
plays.title: Compare a move using take-home pay and actual expenses
plays.text: Build two monthly budgets using your present location and the proposed one. Include housing quotes, commuting, insurance, childcare, utilities, and travel to people you would still visit. Add deposits, overlap between leases, moving costs, and a job-transition reserve. Ask payroll about benefits and withholding, and check both states' revenue departments for residency and remote-work rules. A state's lack of income tax does not make every household's total costs lower.
plays.cost: Estimate: two to four hours initially; multistate work or unusual residency facts may justify paid tax advice before committing.
plays.payoff: The comparison shows which costs could absorb a pay increase and how much cash the transition itself requires.
plays.basis: Practice / Guidance. [Consumer.gov budgeting guide](https://consumer.gov/your-money/making-budget), [IRS directory of state government tax resources](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/state-government-websites).

plays.title: Verify an interstate mover before paying a deposit
plays.text: Check the mover's registration and complaint information through FMCSA, and confirm whether you are dealing with a carrier or a broker. plays.chapterTitle: Make major commitments with a full-cost plan
plays.title: Test transportation alternatives before selling a car
plays.text: Price a realistic month of transit, walking or cycling where safe, carpooling, occasional rentals, and paid rides. Include late shifts, bad weather, accessibility needs, childcare trips, and emergencies. Compare that total with the car costs you would actually eliminate. Try the alternative routine while you still have a fallback; a route that works for one commute may fail for the rest of your household's life.
plays.cost: Estimate: one hour to plan and a one- to two-week trial; fares, rentals, equipment, and backup rides vary locally.
plays.payoff: A practical trial reveals whether fewer cars, fewer driving days, or a different location fits your time and budget.
plays.basis: Practice / Guidance. Transportation availability and safety are local. [EPA transportation alternatives](https://www.epa.gov/transportation-air-pollution-and-climate-change/what-you-can-do-reduce-pollution-vehicles-and).

plays.chapterTitle: Make major commitments with a full-cost plan
plays.title: Separate the celebration budget from the life after it
plays.text: Before a wedding, a planned addition to the family, or another large commitment, price the ongoing household change alongside the upfront event. Use actual quotes and your benefits documents for childcare, leave, medical cost sharing, housing, and insurance where relevant. Agree on a spending ceiling and which costs can be postponed. plays.cost: Estimate: a 60–90 minute household discussion, followed by collecting quotes; the planning worksheet can be free and revisited monthly.
plays.payoff: You can see whether a one-time purchase competes with recurring needs and decide consciously where to spend or scale back.

plays.title: Put the scope and changes in writing

plays.chapterTitle: Turn retirement savings into a workable income plan
plays.title: Track required distributions account by account
plays.text: Create an inventory of retirement accounts and ask each administrator which required minimum distribution rules apply for the current year. Confirm the starting deadline using your birth date, account type, employment status, and whether you inherited the account. Do not assume one withdrawal satisfies every account's requirement. Roth accounts generally have no lifetime RMD for the original owner, but inherited accounts have separate rules. Confirm completed withdrawals before the relevant deadlines.
plays.cost: Estimate: one to two hours for the inventory and annual check; inherited accounts or complex tax situations may need paid professional advice.
plays.payoff: You can identify different deadlines and distribution obligations before a missed or misdirected withdrawal creates a problem.

Use the resulting range to identify employers to approach and questions to ask, rather than anchoring on a single headline salary.

plays.title: Make a specific compensation request before accepting
plays.text: After receiving an offer, ask about the decision deadline and which terms can change. Prepare one concise request tied to relevant experience, responsibilities, and market evidence. Rank base pay, schedule, leave, start date, relocation support, and professional development by their value to you. Use the comparison in chapter 13.5 to check the full package. Avoid inventing another offer, and obtain agreed changes in writing before accepting; some employers and pay systems have little flexibility.
plays.cost: Estimate one hour to prepare and a short conversation; no paid negotiation service is necessary.
plays.payoff: May improve an offer or reveal constraints that change whether the job fits your needs.
plays.basis: Guidance and Practice. [University of Michigan salary and negotiation guidance](https://careercenter.umich.edu/article/salary-and-relocation-information).

plays.title: Choose the smallest credible training step toward a real job
plays.text: Pick a target role and compare its typical duties and entry requirements in the Occupational Outlook Handbook with local openings. Identify one missing skill or credential that employers actually request. Compare employer training, public workforce programs, a short course, and the apprenticeships in chapter 15.2. Ask a state workforce office about eligibility and approved funding before enrolling. A certificate is useful only if the relevant employers or licensing bodies recognize it; program availability and support vary.

plays.payoff: Helps direct training money toward a concrete requirement and may uncover lower-cost routes.

plays.title: Build a small portfolio that shows your contribution

plays.title: Keep a job-search kit ready while you are employed

Keep credentials and personal contact information accessible outside an employer account. plays.payoff: Reduces administrative delay when an opportunity or job loss arrives, without making layoffs predictable.

plays.title: Check reuse rights before publishing someone else's work
plays.text: For each image, article, song, code component, or template, record who created it and the permission or license that covers your intended use. Follow restrictions and required notices; credit alone does not establish permission. When relying on fair use, evaluate the actual circumstances instead of a supposed safe word count or percentage. plays.cost: Estimate 15–30 minutes for a small project's rights inventory; licenses or legal advice may add cost.
plays.payoff: Makes reuse decisions traceable and can prevent an avoidable takedown or expensive rework later.

plays.title: Disclose paid and affiliate relationships where people will notice
plays.text: When recommending something because of payment, an affiliate arrangement, employment, or a free product, disclose the relevant connection clearly with the endorsement. plays.cost: Usually free; estimate a few minutes per post and a review when formats or partnerships change.
plays.payoff: Gives readers context for your recommendation and reduces avoidable advertising-compliance problems.

plays.title: Check refund rights before accepting an airline voucher
plays.text: If an airline cancels or significantly changes a covered flight, save the original and revised itinerary and decide whether you still want to travel. Read the current rule and the seller's instructions before accepting a voucher. Your voluntary cancellation of a nonrefundable ticket is a different situation. A refund right also does not mean every delay requires cash compensation.
plays.cost: Checking the rule is free; estimate 20–30 minutes for documentation and the first contact.
plays.payoff: Helps you choose knowingly between replacement travel, credit, and any refund you are entitled to receive.

plays.title: Verify the lodging and cancellation terms before paying
plays.text: Confirm the property and booking contact independently, especially for an unfamiliar vacation rental. Save the total price, deposit terms, cancellation deadline and time zone, check-in requirements, and any separate fees before payment. Ask for a written rental agreement and use the property's or platform's verified payment process. A request to move a booking into wire transfers, gift cards, or a rushed private transaction is a reason to stop. A convincing listing or confirmation email alone does not establish ownership.
plays.cost: Estimate 15 minutes before booking; verification can require a phone call using an independently found number.
plays.payoff: Reduces preventable booking misunderstandings and exposure to rental scams, without guaranteeing the property or refund.

plays.title: Preserve the credit-card billing-dispute deadline
plays.text: Contact the card issuer immediately when you find an error. To preserve federal billing-error rights, ensure your written notice reaches the designated billing-inquiries address within 60 calendar days after the issuer sent the first statement showing the error. Keep copies and delivery evidence. Do not let a merchant's investigation consume that deadline. Report suspected unauthorized use promptly too. Debit-card disputes and defective-goods complaints can follow different rules; identify the issue rather than assuming every chargeback works alike.
plays.cost: Estimate 30 minutes to assemble statements, receipts, correspondence, and the notice; postage may cost a few dollars.
plays.payoff: Preserves an available dispute procedure; it does not guarantee the issuer will decide in your favor.
plays.basis: Rule and Guidance. [CFPB credit-card billing disputes](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-dispute-a-charge-on-my-credit-card-bill-en-61/); [Regulation Z notice requirements](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/13/).

plays.title: Read your state's small-claims procedure before filing
plays.text: Use the official court website for the place where the case belongs. Check eligible claims, dollar limits, filing deadlines, proper defendant names, service requirements, fees, and any demand-letter prerequisite. Organize a dated timeline and evidence supporting the amount requested. Consider whether settlement would be practical and whether a judgment could actually be collected. Maine's court guide illustrates these procedural steps, but its rules are not national rules. Being sued also requires a timely response even if you believe the claim is wrong.
plays.cost: Estimate two hours for initial preparation; court, service, travel, and collection costs vary, with possible fee waivers.
plays.payoff: Helps you decide whether the process fits the dispute and avoid preventable filing mistakes.

plays.title: Confirm health coverage through each life transition
plays.text: Ask the plan administrator what happens when you turn 18, leave school, move, start a job, or approach 26. If a parent's plan offers dependent coverage, federal rules generally allow you to remain on it until 26, but confirm the exact end date and local provider network. Medicaid and CHIP have separate eligibility and renewal rules. Read state notices and evaluate replacement coverage early; a birthday, new address, or old insurance card does not prove continued enrollment.
plays.cost: Estimate 30–60 minutes to confirm dates, costs, and options; premiums and eligibility depend on the plan and household.
plays.payoff: Helps maintain usable coverage during a transition and exposes gaps before you need an appointment.

plays.title: Check voter registration through your official election office
plays.text: If eligible to vote, use Vote.gov to reach your state or territory's registration instructions. Check your registration after moving or changing your name, and verify the deadline, accepted identification, and available voting methods well before the election. Rules differ by jurisdiction; online registration and same-day registration are not universal. Obtain polling-place and ballot-return information from your election office instead of a forwarded post. If an eligibility question applies to you, ask the office or qualified local assistance directly.
plays.cost: Registration is free; estimate 10–20 minutes for a status check and any needed update.
plays.payoff: Gives you time to resolve a record problem and make a voting plan that fits local rules.

plays.title: Name a medical decision-maker before an emergency

plays.title: Use a thermometer and refrigerate perishable food promptly
plays.text: Keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food, clean hands and preparation surfaces, and use a food thermometer with the recommended temperature for the food. Refrigerate perishables within two hours, or one hour when exposed to temperatures above 90°F. Thaw safely in the refrigerator, cold water, or microwave; cook immediately after thawing in cold water or the microwave. Appearance and smell cannot reliably establish safety, and a bargain is not worth eating recalled food.
plays.cost: A food thermometer has a modest upfront cost; safe handling adds attention.
plays.payoff: Reduces avoidable food poisoning and wasted meals.
